focus.text: Agreement is a small ending that carries a lot of trust. In the present, a singular subject takes a verb with -s and a plural subject does not, and *be* changes shape in the past as well. The difficulty is rarely the rule itself; it is finding the real subject when a phrase or a clause sits between it and the verb. Cover everything between the subject and the verb with your finger, and the right form is usually obvious.

summaryTable.caption: Which verb form goes with which subject
rows: he / she / it, a singular noun
I / you / we / they, a plural noun
**There is** one exit. **There are** two exits.

pretest.sentence: There are three computers in the small study room.
pretest.reason: *Computers* is plural, so *there are* is right.

pretest.sentence: Many people in my neighbourhood is worried about flooding.
pretest.reason: *People* is plural, so the verb is *are*.

pretest.sentence: Each of the classrooms has its own projector.
pretest.reason: *Each* is singular, even before a plural noun.

pretest.sentence: The price of vegetables have risen sharply this month.
pretest.reason: The head noun is *the price*, not *vegetables*, so write *has risen*.

pretest.sentence: There have a new bookshop near the bus station.
My parents work in Đà Nẵng, but my sister works in Huế.
pretest.reason: A plural subject takes the base verb and a singular subject takes -s.

pretest.sentence: One of my classmates are studying in Australia.
pretest.reason: The subject is *one*, not *classmates*, so write *is studying*.

pretest.sentence: Neither of the two plans solves the problem completely.
pretest.reason: *Neither of* takes a singular verb in formal writing.

pretest.sentence: Learning two foreign languages take a lot of time.
pretest.reason: A gerund subject (*learning two foreign languages*) is singular: *takes*.

pretest.sentence: The team of researchers was divided about the results.
pretest.reason: The head noun is *the team*, acting here as one body, so the verb is singular.

context.title: The Saturday clean-up
context.paragraph: Every Saturday morning a group of students from our school meets at the park gate. The leader of the two teams is Ngân, and she brings the gloves and the bags. There are always more volunteers in the dry season, but neither rain nor heat stops the regulars. One of the teams collects plastic along the canal, while the other cuts the grass around the benches. Each volunteer writes the weight of the rubbish in a notebook, because the numbers help the club ask for money. Working together for two hours every week is hard, yet everybody says the park looks better. The staff of the park now know all our names.

sections.title: Forming agreement in the present

table.caption: Present verb forms after singular and plural subjects

notes: In the past, only *be* changes: *I / he / she / it **was***, *you / we / they **were***. Every other past verb has one form for all subjects.

items.stem: The new sports hall ___ open until nine every evening.
items.reason: *The sports hall* is it, so the present verb takes -s.

items.stem: My two older brothers ___ in a factory near Biên Hòa.
items.reason: A plural subject takes the base verb with no -s.

items.stem: There ___ several reasons for the delay.
items.reason: *Reasons* is plural, so *there are* is correct.

items.stem: Each of the four groups ___ a different topic.
items.reason: *Each* is singular, even before a plural noun.

items.stem: The number of students in my class ___ thirty-two.
items.reason: The head noun is *the number*, so the verb is singular.

sections.title: Forming *there is* and *there are*

table.caption: there is and there are across time
rows: There **is** a market on this street.
There **are** two markets on this street.

notes: English uses *there is* and *there are* to say that something exists. *There have* is never possible, even though many languages use one word for *have* and for *there is*.
tips: *There* starts the sentence, but it is not the subject. Look to the right of the verb to decide between *is* and *are*.

sections.title: Using agreement when other words get in the way

rules.text: Find the head of the subject and ignore everything between it and the verb.

examples.text: The cost of school uniforms **has** risen every year.
Students who join the club **get** a free notebook.

rules.text: *Each*, *every*, *one of*, *everybody* and *nobody* are singular, even when a plural noun follows.

examples.text: Each of the classes **has** its own timetable.
One of my cousins **lives** in Cần Thơ.

rules.text: *People*, *police*, *children* and *staff* are plural, so they take a plural verb.

examples.text: Many people **walk** to the market in the early morning.
The police **were** already at the scene.

items.stem: The list of approved books ___ on the noticeboard.
items.reason: The head noun is *the list*, not *books*.

items.stem: There ___ a lot of noise from the building site every morning.
items.reason: *Noise* is uncountable, so the singular *there is* is correct.

items.stem: Young people in my city ___ more about climate change than before.
items.reason: *People* is plural, so the verb has no -s.

items.stem: One of the teachers ___ us to enter the competition.
items.reason: The subject is *one*, so the verb is singular.

items.stem: Every student and every teacher ___ a copy of the timetable.
items.reason: Subjects introduced by *every* stay singular, even when they are joined by *and*.

sections.title: Using *there is* and *there are*

rules.text: Use *there is* or *there are* to introduce something new, and make the verb agree with the noun that follows it.

examples.text: **There are** four bus routes from my village to the city centre.
**There is** a long queue outside the exam hall.

rules.text: With a list, the verb agrees with the first item.

examples.text: **There is** a laptop, two chargers and a printer in the cupboard.

rules.text: Keep *have* for possession. It never means that something exists.

examples.text: **There are** many parks in Đà Nẵng, and my family **has** a favourite one.

notes: In writing, prefer a full verb where you can: *Đà Nẵng **has** many parks* is stronger than *There are many parks in Đà Nẵng*.

sections.title: Using agreement with harder subjects

rules.text: Treat a collective noun (*team, government, family, company*) as singular when it acts as one body, and as plural when the members act separately.

examples.text: The committee **were** unable to agree among themselves.

rules.text: With *either … or* and *neither … nor*, the verb agrees with the noun closest to it.

examples.text: Neither the teachers nor the head **wants** to cancel the trip.
Either the bus or the trains **are** late every morning.

rules.text: A gerund or a clause used as a subject is singular, however long it is.

examples.text: **Cycling** to school every day **saves** my family a lot of money.
What most students want **is** more time for revision.

rules.text: With *a number of* the verb is plural, but with *the number of* it is singular.

examples.text: A number of students **have** asked for extra lessons.
The number of students **has** doubled since 2019.

notes: Quantifiers with *of* take their number from the noun after *of*: *some of the water **is** warm*, *some of the seats **are** free*.
tips: Long subjects hide their head noun. In *the effect of social media on young readers*, the head is *the effect*, so the verb is singular.

items.sentence: The list of problems are getting longer every week.
items.reason: The head noun is *the list*, so the verb is singular.

items.sentence: There have a big supermarket at the end of our street.
items.reason: Existence takes *there is* or *there are*, never *have*.

items.sentence: Neither of the two routes are shorter than ten kilometres.
items.reason: *Neither of* takes a singular verb in formal writing.

items.sentence: Reading news articles in English help me learn new vocabulary.
items.reason: A gerund subject (*reading news articles in English*) is singular.

items.sentence: Many people in my class thinks that the test was too long.
items.reason: *People* is plural, so the verb has no -s.

editing.text: There have two secondary schools in the small town where I live. The number of students in each class are about forty, so the classrooms are always noisy. Each of my three brothers study in a different year, and one of them are preparing for the entrance exam. My mother, who works at the post office, leave home before seven every day. Many people in our street walks to work, because the bus only comes twice an hour. Neither my father nor my uncle drive a car, so the whole family shares one old motorbike. Reading about big cities make me curious about life there. There is three new shops near the market this year, and my friends say that the town is changing fast.

errors.span: in each class are about forty
errors.fix: in each class is about forty
errors.reason: The head noun is *the number*, so the verb is singular.
*Each of* is singular, so the verb takes -s.
The subject is *my mother*; the relative clause between them changes nothing.
*People* is plural, so the verb has no -s.
With *neither … nor*, the verb agrees with the nearer subject (*my uncle*).
*Three new shops* is plural, so use *there are*.

topics.prompt: Write an email to a host family before an exchange visit. Describe who is in your family, what each of them does, and what there is to see in your home town.
checklist: Every present verb after a singular subject ends in -s.
*There is* and *there are* agree with the noun that follows them.
*Each of* and *one of* take a singular verb.

topics.prompt: "Every student should do two hours of sport a week." Give your view and support it with reasons.
checklist: Subjects such as *students*, *people* and *the number of students* take the verb they really need.
At least one sentence has a phrase between the subject and the verb (*the cost of sports clubs is…*).
At least one sentence uses a gerund subject (*playing football helps…*).

topics.prompt: Write a short report about a club, team or class you belong to: how many members there are, what the group does each week, and what the members think of it.
checklist: The collective noun (*team*, *group*, *club*) keeps one number through the whole report.
*There is* and *there are* introduce the numbers correctly.
*Neither … nor* or *either … or* appears at least once with the right verb.
